title: Triton and tile-based GPU programming
why: Triton is how most new production kernels get written at OpenAI, Meta and in TorchInductor. Programming whole tiles instead of threads is the mental model the frontier works in; you already wrote a codegen backend, now learn the one industry uses.

steps.title: Tillet, Kung, Cox: Triton (MAPL 2019)
steps.detail: Sections 3-5: Triton-C, Triton-IR, the tile-level optimization passes. Compare with your own IR.

steps.title: Triton tutorial 01: Vector Addition
steps.detail: Learn program_id, masks, BLOCK_SIZE as constexpr; run the benchmark and plot GB/s vs. size.

steps.title: Triton tutorial 02: Fused Softmax
steps.detail: Row-per-program reduction; note why fusion makes this memory-bound kernel ~2x faster than eager torch.

steps.title: Triton tutorial 03: Matrix Multiplication
steps.detail: Block tiling, L2 'grouped ordering' of program ids, autotune configs. Reach >=80% of cuBLAS on fp16.

steps.title: Triton tutorial 04: Low-Memory Dropout
steps.detail: Counter-based Philox RNG in-kernel: recompute masks instead of storing them.

steps.title: Triton tutorial 05: Layer Normalization
steps.detail: Forward and backward; the backward's two-stage parallel reduction of dW/db with locks is the hard part.

steps.title: Triton tutorial 06: Fused Attention
steps.detail: FlashAttention-2 in Triton: online softmax, causal masking stages. Read alongside the papers below.

steps.title: Triton-Puzzles (Sasha Rush)
steps.detail: Do all puzzles through Flash Attention and the quantized matmul; they force you to reason about shapes and masks without a GPU.

steps.title: FlashAttention (Dao et al. 2022)
steps.detail: Sections 2-3: IO-aware tiling, recomputation. Derive the HBM-access bound yourself.

steps.title: FlashAttention-2
steps.detail: Sections 3.1-3.3: work partitioning across warps and sequence-length parallelism.

steps.title: Horace He, Making Deep Learning Go Brrrr
steps.detail: Compute vs. memory vs. overhead bound: use this lens on every kernel you benchmark.

steps.title: Port one of your compiler's kernels to a Triton backend
steps.detail: Add a Triton codegen target to your compiler for elementwise+reduce fusions; diff results vs. your CUDA backend.

build: A Triton backend for your compiler (elementwise, reduction and matmul codegen) plus all six tutorials reproduced with benchmark plots.
check: Tutorial 03 matmul reaches >=80% of cuBLAS fp16 TFLOPS at 4096^2
Fused attention matches torch SDPA to 1e-2 (fp16) for causal and non-causal
Your compiler emits Triton for a fused LayerNorm and it passes your test suite
You can explain grouped program ordering and why it raises L2 hit rate
outcomes: After this module you can write, autotune and profile Triton kernels for matmul, reductions and attention
After this module you can reason about tile shapes, num_warps and num_stages from roofline numbers instead of guessing
After this module you can generate Triton from your own compiler IR
After this module you can read and modify FlashAttention-style kernels
stuck: Wrong results only at odd sizes: you forgot a mask on load or store; test sizes like 1000 and 4097, not just powers of two
Autotune 'wins' that vanish: you benchmarked with a cold cache or included compilation; use triton.testing.do_bench
Layernorm backward races: re-read the lock/atomic section of tutorial 05 before inventing your own reduction
Attention numerically off: check you rescale the running accumulator when the running max changes (FA2 paper, Alg. 1)
Puzzles confusing: print shapes with the interpreter mode (TRITON_INTERPRET=1) on CPU

project.title: Fused kernel library: beat torch.compile on three real ops
project.brief: Pick three ops that appear in a real model (e.g. RMSNorm+residual, rotary embedding fused into QKV projection, SwiGLU, fused cross-entropy over a large vocab). Write Triton kernels with forward and backward, autotune them, and drop them into a nanoGPT-sized model. Show end-to-end training step speedup against eager and torch.compile.
deliverables: repo with kernels, gradcheck tests and a pip-installable package
README with roofline plots (achieved GB/s or TFLOPS vs. peak) across sizes
a 600–1200 word write-up explaining each fusion, the bound it hits and what limited further gains

rubric.solid: All three kernels pass gradcheck; each is >=1.3x eager and within 10% of torch.compile; roofline plot per kernel
rubric.exceptional: At least one kernel beats torch.compile by >=1.2x end to end, e.g. a chunked fused cross-entropy that cuts peak memory by >2x, with Nsight Compute evidence for why

references.title: Liger Kernel (fused Triton kernels for LLM training)

title: CUTLASS, CuTe and Hopper/Blackwell features
why: The fastest kernels on H100/B200 (FlashAttention-3, cuBLAS-class GEMMs) use TMA, wgmma and warp specialization, which Triton only partly exposes. Teams writing inference kernels expect you to read and write CuTe layouts.

steps.title: Simon Boehm, How to Optimize a CUDA Matmul Kernel
steps.detail: Re-derive kernels 1-10 quickly as a warm-up; this is the baseline vocabulary for the rest.

steps.title: CuTe quickstart (CUTLASS docs)
steps.detail: Then read 01_layout, 02_layout_algebra, 03_tensor, 0x_gemm_tutorial in the same folder.

steps.title: CuTe docs folder: layout algebra exercises
steps.detail: Hand-compute composition, complement and logical_divide on 2-3 layouts; check with cute::print.

steps.title: Colfax: CUTLASS tutorial, design of a GEMM kernel
steps.detail: Mainloop/epilogue split, pipelining stages, how CUTLASS composes collectives.

steps.title: Colfax: Mastering the NVIDIA Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA)
steps.detail: TMA descriptors, multicast, mbarrier synchronization.

steps.title: Colfax: Fast matrix multiplication using wgmma
steps.detail: Warpgroup MMA, smem layout requirements, async fences.

steps.title: PTX ISA: wgmma and cp.async.bulk sections
steps.detail: Look up wgmma.mma_async and cp.async.bulk.tensor; see exactly what CuTe emits.

steps.title: FlashAttention-3
steps.detail: Sections 3.1-3.3: producer/consumer warp specialization, ping-pong scheduling, FP8 incoherent processing.

steps.title: ThunderKittens paper
steps.detail: Tile primitives as a middle ground between Triton and CUTLASS; compare abstractions.

steps.title: ThunderKittens: build and run an example kernel
steps.detail: Run the H100 GEMM/attention example; profile with Nsight Compute and identify the pipeline.

steps.title: Write a Hopper GEMM in CuTe
steps.detail: TMA load -> smem -> wgmma, 2-4 stage pipeline, then add warp specialization. No GPU with sm90? Rent one by the hour.

build: A from-scratch CuTe GEMM for H100 progressing from SIMT to wgmma+TMA+warp-specialized, each step benchmarked.
check: Final GEMM reaches >=70% of cuBLAS bf16 at 8192^2 on H100
You can draw the CuTe layout (shape:stride) of an smem tile with swizzle
You can explain why warp specialization helps when TMA is async
Nsight Compute report shows tensor-core utilization per version
outcomes: After this module you can read and write CuTe layouts and layout algebra
After this module you can build a TMA+wgmma pipelined GEMM on Hopper
After this module you can explain FlashAttention-3's scheduling and reproduce part of it
After this module you can choose between Triton, ThunderKittens and CUTLASS for a given kernel
stuck: Template error walls: compile tiny examples first and use cute::print/print_latex to inspect layouts
wgmma hangs or garbage: missing fence/commit/wait or wrong smem swizzle; compare with the Colfax wgmma post line by line
No Hopper GPU: do the layout and SIMT parts locally, then rent an H100 for a few hours with a script ready
TMA descriptor errors: global tensor must be 16-byte aligned and strides multiples of 16 bytes
Lost in CUTLASS 3 collectives: read the Colfax GEMM design post before the source

project.title: FP8 or bf16 attention/GEMM on Hopper with a public benchmark
project.brief: Implement a warp-specialized Hopper kernel for a real workload: either a grouped GEMM for MoE layers or a decode-time attention kernel (paged KV). Benchmark against cuBLAS/FlashAttention-3/FlashInfer across shapes taken from Llama or DeepSeek configs, and document every optimization with profiler evidence.
deliverables: repo with the kernel, a PyTorch extension binding and correctness tests
README with TFLOPS tables vs. baselines across >=6 real shapes
a 600–1200 word write-up walking through the pipeline, layouts and the remaining gap

rubric.solid: >=60% of the best public baseline on all shapes, correct to fp tolerance, profiler screenshots
rubric.exceptional: Matches or beats the baseline on some shapes (e.g. small-batch decode) and explains why with occupancy/pipeline analysis; upstreamable quality

title: Industrial ML compilers: MLIR, XLA/StableHLO, TorchInductor, TVM
why: Every big lab's stack is one of these. You built a toy compiler; now read real designs, see which choices they made differently, and get fluent in MLIR, the lingua franca of accelerator compilers.

steps.title: MLIR: Scaling Compiler Infrastructure (Lattner et al.)
steps.detail: Sections 2-4: dialects, regions, progressive lowering.

steps.title: j2kun mlir-tutorial: Getting started
steps.detail: Build with Bazel or CMake; get mlir-opt running.

steps.title: j2kun: Running and testing a lowering
steps.detail: lit/FileCheck tests; you'll use them for everything.

steps.title: j2kun: Writing our first pass
steps.detail: An affine loop-unroll pass and a rewrite pattern.

steps.title: j2kun: Defining a new dialect
steps.detail: TableGen ops/types: the basis for your toy tensor dialect.

steps.title: j2kun: Canonicalizers and declarative rewrite patterns
steps.detail: DRR patterns for algebraic simplification.

steps.title: j2kun: Dialect conversion
steps.detail: Type converters and conversion targets: lower your dialect to arith/linalg.

steps.title: j2kun: Lowering through LLVM
steps.detail: Finish the pipeline to an executable.

steps.title: OpenXLA architecture and StableHLO
steps.detail: HLO, fusion and layout assignment; then skim the StableHLO spec at openxla.org/stablehlo.

steps.title: TorchInductor design post (Jason Ansel)
steps.detail: Define-by-run loop IR, scheduling, Triton codegen. Then the PyTorch 2 paper sections on Dynamo and Inductor.

steps.title: PyTorch 2 paper (ASPLOS 2024)
steps.detail: Sections 3-5: graph capture via bytecode, guards, Inductor.

steps.title: TVM (OSDI 2018)
steps.detail: Sections 3-5: tensor expressions, schedules, learned cost model.

build: A toy 'tg' MLIR dialect (add, mul, matmul, reduce) with canonicalization and a lowering to linalg -> loops -> LLVM, tested with FileCheck.
check: mlir-opt runs your pass pipeline and the resulting binary computes a correct matmul
At least 10 FileCheck tests cover canonicalization and lowering
One-page comparison table: your compiler vs. XLA vs. Inductor vs. TVM on IR levels, fusion, scheduling, autotuning
You can dump and read Inductor's generated Triton for a small model (TORCH_LOGS=output_code)
outcomes: After this module you can define an MLIR dialect, write passes and lower to LLVM
After this module you can read XLA HLO and Inductor output and explain their fusion decisions
After this module you can compare compiler designs in an interview with specifics
After this module you can navigate a large compiler codebase to find where a decision is made
stuck: Build takes forever: use the tutorial's pinned LLVM commit and ccache; build once, release mode
TableGen errors are opaque: start from the tutorial's dialect and change one thing at a time
Dialect conversion 'failed to legalize': mark the right ops legal/illegal and check your type converter covers block args
Inductor output overwhelming: start with a two-op function and TORCH_LOGS=output_code,schedule

project.title: Port your compiler's frontend onto MLIR (or upstream-style Inductor study)
project.brief: Make your course compiler emit your MLIR dialect, then reuse upstream linalg tiling/fusion and the GPU dialect to reach a GPU, and compare against your hand-written backend. Alternative: a deep empirical study of TorchInductor fusion decisions on 5 HuggingFace models with a minimal patch that improves one case.
deliverables: repo with the dialect, passes, FileCheck tests and an end-to-end example
README with performance comparison vs. your original backend and vs. torch.compile
a 600–1200 word write-up on what MLIR made easier or harder than your own IR

rubric.solid: An MLP runs end to end through MLIR with correct results; 20+ lit tests
rubric.exceptional: A small transformer block runs on GPU via MLIR within 2x of torch.compile, or the Inductor patch is opened upstream with benchmarks

title: Scheduling theory: polyhedral model and auto-schedulers
why: Your BEAM search picked schedules by trial. Research compilers reason about the space formally (polyhedra, dependences) or learn cost models. Grad labs and XLA/TPU teams expect you to know both camps.

steps.title: Halide (PLDI 2013)
steps.detail: Sections 3-5: algorithm/schedule separation, the tradeoff space of locality, parallelism and recompute.

steps.title: Learning to Optimize Halide with Tree Search and Random Programs (2019)
steps.detail: Beam search + learned cost model; compare with your BEAM.

steps.title: Ansor (OSDI 2020)
steps.detail: Sections 4-6: sketch generation, random annotation, evolutionary fine-tuning.

steps.title: isl tutorial (Verdoolaege)
steps.detail: Sets, maps, dependences, schedule trees. Work the examples with islpy.

steps.title: Pluto: polyhedral source-to-source
steps.detail: Read the Pluto paper linked there; run it on a stencil and matmul and inspect tiling hyperplanes.

steps.title: Tiramisu (CGO 2019)
steps.detail: A polyhedral compiler with a scheduling language: the bridge between Halide and isl.

steps.title: Dependence analysis in your compiler
steps.detail: Using islpy, compute dependences for your loop IR and prove which tile/permute transforms are legal.

steps.title: Learned cost model for your BEAM search
steps.detail: Collect (schedule features, runtime) pairs, train a small GBDT/MLP, and use it to prune search.

build: islpy-based legality checking for your loop transforms, plus a learned cost model that cuts BEAM search time.
check: Your compiler rejects an illegal interchange on a loop-carried dependence and accepts the legal one
Cost-model-guided search finds schedules within 10% of exhaustive BEAM using <=25% of the measurements
You can write the iteration domain and schedule of a tiled matmul as isl sets/maps
One-page comparison of Halide autoscheduler vs. Ansor vs. polyhedral
outcomes: After this module you can model loop nests as polyhedra and check transform legality
After this module you can build and evaluate a learned cost model for schedule search
After this module you can explain the design space of auto-schedulers and their failure modes
After this module you can read a scheduling paper and reproduce its key experiment
stuck: isl notation feels alien: write every example by hand first, then check with islpy
Cost model overfits: split by program, not by schedule, or you measure leakage
Measurements noisy: lock clocks, warm up, take medians of repeated runs
Pluto build issues: use a container; the concepts matter more than the tool

project.title: Reproduce a cost-model result on your own compiler
project.brief: Reproduce the core claim of a learned-scheduling paper (Halide 2019, Ansor, or TenSet) inside your compiler: same feature ideas, your search space. Report sample efficiency curves and transfer across GPUs or across ops.
deliverables: repo with the dataset of measured schedules (released), training code and integration
README with search-time vs. achieved-performance curves against random and plain BEAM
a 600–1200 word write-up on what transferred, what didn't and why

rubric.solid: Dataset of >=20k measured schedules, cost model with reported rank correlation, clear sample-efficiency plot
rubric.exceptional: Shows cross-hardware transfer or a novel feature that measurably helps; written like a workshop paper

title: Numerics and low precision
why: Inference cost is dominated by bytes moved, so every frontier serving stack runs fp8, int4 or MX formats. Knowing exactly where precision is lost, and how to recover it, is a top skill in inference and kernel teams.

steps.title: Fabien Sanglard, Floating point visually explained
steps.detail: Warm-up; then derive bf16, fp16, fp8 E4M3/E5M2 ranges by hand.

steps.title: FP8 Formats for Deep Learning (Micikevicius et al.)
steps.detail: E4M3 vs E5M2, scaling, which tensors get which format.

steps.title: OCP Microscaling (MX) Formats v1.0 spec
steps.detail: Sections 5-6: shared E8M0 block scale, MXFP8/6/4 and MXINT8 element encodings.

steps.title: Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning
steps.detail: Empirical results for MX training and inference.

steps.title: LLM.int8()
steps.detail: Outlier features and mixed-precision decomposition.

steps.title: SmoothQuant
steps.detail: Migrating activation outliers into weights; derive the scaling factor alpha.

steps.title: GPTQ
steps.detail: OBQ-style second-order rounding; sections 3-4 incl. the lazy batch updates and Cholesky trick.

steps.title: AWQ
steps.detail: Activation-aware per-channel scaling; compare with GPTQ.

steps.title: FP8 training recipe in Transformer Engine
steps.detail: Read the FP8 docs and delayed-scaling recipe; run the example on a small model.

steps.title: Bit-exact format emulators
steps.detail: Write numpy emulators for bf16, fp8 E4M3/E5M2 and MXFP4 (round-to-nearest-even, saturation), tested against torch.float8 dtypes.

steps.title: Quantized matmul kernel
steps.detail: W4A16 Triton kernel with in-kernel dequantization; add it to your compiler as a dtype.

build: Format emulators, GPTQ and AWQ implemented from scratch on a ~1B model, and a W4A16 kernel used by your compiler.
check: Emulators bit-match torch.float8_e4m3fn/e5m2 casts on 1e6 random values
Your GPTQ 4-bit model is within 0.5 perplexity of the reference implementation on WikiText-2
W4A16 kernel is faster than fp16 at batch 1 decode shapes
You can explain why E4M3 has no infinity and what that means for scaling
outcomes: After this module you can derive and emulate any fp/MX format bit-exactly
After this module you can implement GPTQ, AWQ and SmoothQuant and diagnose accuracy loss
After this module you can write fused dequant-matmul kernels
After this module you can design a precision recipe for a model and defend it with numbers
stuck: Emulator off by one ulp: you truncated instead of round-to-nearest-even, or mishandled subnormals
GPTQ blows up: add damping to the Hessian diagonal (the paper uses 1% of the mean)
Perplexity numbers don't match papers: same eval context length, dataset split and tokenizer
Quantized kernel slow: dequantize in registers after loading packed ints, not into smem

project.title: Precision study: how low can a real LLM go?
project.brief: Take an open 1-8B model and build a systematic study across bf16, fp8 (per-tensor vs. per-channel), MXFP8/MXFP4 and int4 (GPTQ vs. AWQ), measuring perplexity, a downstream task and real throughput with your kernels. Find which layers are sensitive and propose a mixed-precision recipe.
deliverables: repo with emulators, quantizers, kernels and an eval harness
README with accuracy-vs-bytes Pareto plot and per-layer sensitivity heatmap
a 600–1200 word write-up of findings and the recommended recipe

rubric.solid: At least 6 configurations evaluated on 2 metrics with measured speed; reproducible scripts
rubric.exceptional: A mixed-precision recipe that Pareto-dominates uniform int4 or MXFP4, with kernel speedups measured, written up as a blog post others cite

title: Accelerator architecture: systolic arrays, TPUs, dataflows
why: A compiler is only as good as its model of the hardware. TPU, Trainium and startup accelerator teams hire people who can reason about dataflow, buffer sizing and utilization, not only GPUs.

steps.title: In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a TPU (TPUv1, ISCA 2017)
steps.detail: Systolic matrix unit, the roofline section, why latency mattered more than throughput.

steps.title: TPU v4 (ISCA 2023)
steps.detail: Optical circuit switches, SparseCores, the scale-up story; contrast with v1.

steps.title: Efficient Processing of DNNs: A Tutorial and Survey (Sze et al.)
steps.detail: Sections on dataflows: weight-, output-, row-stationary.

steps.title: Eyeriss (JSSC 2017)
steps.detail: Row-stationary dataflow and energy accounting per memory level.

steps.title: MIT 6.5930 Hardware Architecture for Deep Learning
steps.detail: Follow the lectures on dataflow and mapping; do the Timeloop labs if available.

steps.title: Timeloop/Accelergy
steps.detail: Map a conv and a matmul onto a modeled accelerator; compare mappings by energy and cycles.

steps.title: Gemmini (Berkeley)
steps.detail: Read the README architecture section: a real open systolic generator with a software stack.

steps.title: Cycle-level systolic array simulator
steps.detail: Python or C++: NxN PEs, weight- and output-stationary modes, SRAM buffers, DMA; count cycles and accesses.

steps.title: Compiler backend for your simulator
steps.detail: Lower your compiler's matmul/conv to tiled instructions for the simulator; pick tile sizes by buffer capacity.

build: A cycle-level systolic array simulator with two dataflows, plus a backend in your compiler that targets it.
check: Simulator matches numpy results and an analytic cycle count for matmul within 5%
You can show utilization vs. matrix shape and explain the drop for small or skinny matrices
Your compiler's tiling for the simulator beats naive tiling on a ResNet layer
You can explain why TPUs use bf16 and large systolic arrays
outcomes: After this module you can model accelerator performance and energy from first principles
After this module you can compare dataflows and choose mappings
After this module you can write a compiler backend for a non-GPU target
After this module you can discuss TPU generations in depth
stuck: Simulator too slow: simulate per tile analytically after validating cycle-exact on small cases
Off-by-skew cycle counts: remember the (N-1) fill and drain of a systolic wavefront
Mapping space huge: use Timeloop's mapper ideas, constrain by buffer capacity first
Energy numbers meaningless: use relative per-level costs from Eyeriss/Sze tables

project.title: Design-space exploration of a transformer accelerator
project.brief: Extend your simulator with a vector unit and on-chip memory hierarchy, then explore array size, buffer size and dataflow for a transformer layer (prefill vs. decode). Use your compiler to generate the mapping and produce Pareto curves of perf/area-proxy/energy.
deliverables: repo with simulator, compiler backend and sweep scripts
README with Pareto plots and a validation section against analytic models
a 600–1200 word write-up recommending a design for decode-heavy serving

rubric.solid: Validated simulator, >=50 design points, clear prefill-vs-decode insight
rubric.exceptional: Results cross-checked against Timeloop or published TPU numbers, plus a non-obvious finding (e.g. a dataflow switch per phase) with quantified benefit

title: Distributed training and inference at scale
why: Frontier models never fit on one GPU. Labs need people who can reason about sharding, communication overlap and serving systems; it is the single most in-demand systems skill right now.

steps.title: How to Scale Your Model (JAX scaling book)
steps.detail: Read the rooflines, sharding and transformer-math chapters; do every exercise.

steps.title: The Ultra-Scale Playbook (Hugging Face)
steps.detail: Data, tensor, pipeline, context and expert parallelism with measurements.

steps.title: ZeRO (Rajbhandari et al.)
steps.detail: Stages 1-3 memory math; then the PyTorch FSDP tutorial below.

steps.title: PyTorch FSDP tutorial
steps.detail: Run it, then profile the all-gather/reduce-scatter overlap.

steps.title: Megatron-LM tensor parallelism
steps.detail: Column/row-parallel MLP and attention; count the all-reduces.

steps.title: GPipe and Megatron 1F1B / interleaved schedules
steps.detail: Section 2: pipeline bubbles, 1F1B, interleaving; GPipe is arXiv 1811.06965.

steps.title: Ring Attention
steps.detail: Blockwise attention across devices with overlapped KV passing.

steps.title: GShard and Switch Transformer
steps.detail: Expert parallelism and all-to-all; Switch is arXiv 2101.03961.

steps.title: vLLM / PagedAttention
steps.detail: KV-cache paging and continuous batching for serving.

steps.title: NCCL source and docs
steps.detail: Ring vs. tree all-reduce algorithms, channels, protocols (LL, LL128, Simple).

steps.title: Mini-parallelism library
steps.detail: From scratch on torch.distributed: ZeRO-3-style sharding, 1F1B pipeline, tensor-parallel MLP; test on 2-8 GPUs.

build: A from-scratch distributed library (FSDP-style sharding, TP, 1F1B pipeline) training a GPT-2-size model on multiple GPUs, with communication profiled.
check: Loss curves match single-GPU training to tolerance for each parallelism
Measured memory per GPU matches your ZeRO math within 10%
Profiler trace shows communication overlapped with compute
You can compute MFU and the pipeline bubble fraction for your runs
outcomes: After this module you can derive memory and communication cost for any parallelism combination
After this module you can implement FSDP, TP and pipeline schedules from scratch
After this module you can profile and fix communication bottlenecks
After this module you can explain serving systems: paged KV, continuous batching, expert parallelism
stuck: Hangs: mismatched collective order across ranks; log every collective with rank and shape
Losses diverge from single-GPU: check gradient scaling by world size and RNG seeding per rank
No multi-GPU box: use torch.distributed with gloo on CPU for correctness, rent 8 GPUs for an afternoon for perf
Pipeline bubbles worse than expected: count microbatches vs. stages (bubble ~ (p-1)/m)

project.title: Scale a model and publish an MFU report
project.brief: Train a 1B-class model on 8 GPUs using your library combined in 2D/3D parallelism, then optimize to the best MFU you can, with ablations of each choice. Optionally add ring attention for long context or expert parallelism for an MoE variant.
deliverables: repo with the library, configs and launch scripts
README with MFU, tokens/s and memory tables across parallelism configs plus profiler traces
a 600–1200 word write-up on what limited scaling and how you fixed it

rubric.solid: >=35% MFU on 8 GPUs with correct convergence and an ablation table
rubric.exceptional: >=45% MFU, or a working long-context/MoE extension, with a scaling analysis that predicts your measured numbers

title: Research, open source and career
why: Hiring managers and grad committees judge evidence: merged PRs in real compilers, a reproduced paper, leaderboard results and clear writing. This module turns your skills into that evidence.

steps.title: Karpathy, A Recipe for Training Neural Networks
steps.detail: The mindset for reproductions: become one with the data, overfit first, verify every step.

steps.title: Simon Peyton Jones, How to Write a Great Research Paper
steps.detail: Apply to your reproduction write-up.

steps.title: Pick and reproduce a recent paper
steps.detail: E.g. KernelBench (linked), a FlashAttention variant or a quantization paper. Match a headline number, then ablate.

steps.title: KernelBench
steps.detail: Solve level-1/2 problems by hand and track speedup; know how LLM kernel agents are evaluated.

steps.title: GPU MODE community and leaderboards
steps.detail: Submit to an active kernel competition; join the Discord reading groups.

steps.title: GPU MODE reference kernels
steps.detail: Problem definitions used by the leaderboards.

steps.title: Land a PR in tinygrad
steps.detail: Read the contributing rules (line count, tests, bounties); start with a bounty or a bug with a failing test.

steps.title: Or land a PR in PyTorch
steps.detail: Inductor/Dynamo 'good first issue' labels; follow the CLA and test instructions.

steps.title: Or Triton / vLLM
steps.detail: Small backend fixes or perf issues; vLLM kernels at github.com/vllm-project/vllm.

steps.title: Portfolio and interview prep
steps.detail: Pin 4-6 project repos; prepare to whiteboard a tiled matmul, a reduction, roofline math, a fusion pass and a sharding cost estimate in 45 minutes each.

build: One reproduced paper with a public report, at least one merged PR in a major ML compiler/runtime, a leaderboard submission and a polished portfolio.
check: A merged (not just opened) PR in tinygrad, PyTorch, Triton, vLLM, JAX/XLA or MLIR
Reproduction repo matches a headline number within the paper's reported variance
A ranked leaderboard submission (GPU MODE or KernelBench-style) with writeup
Mock interview: you can derive roofline numbers and write a correct tiled kernel live
outcomes: After this module you can reproduce and extend a systems paper end to end
After this module you can work effectively in a large open-source compiler codebase and get changes merged
After this module you can present your work in writing and interviews at a top-lab bar
After this module you can pick a research direction and justify it with evidence

project.title: Capstone: a research-grade contribution
project.brief: Combine a reproduction with a new idea: e.g. extend a kernel paper to a new hardware or precision, or a scheduling result to a new compiler, and upstream the useful part. Present it as a short paper plus a talk.
deliverables: repo with code, scripts and data to reproduce every figure
README with headline results and links to merged PRs

rubric.solid: Reproduction matches, one merged PR, paper with clear claims and ablations
rubric.exceptional: A novel result accepted at a workshop (e.g. MLSys, NeurIPS workshop) or a feature merged upstream that maintainers use, plus a talk at GPU MODE or a reading group
